question: Why can a linear circuit driven by a single sine be analysed with complex numbers instead of time steps?
options: Because every voltage and current settles to a sine of the same frequency, described by an amplitude and a phase
Because capacitors and inductors disappear at AC
Because complex numbers are faster for computers
Because the circuit stops changing
explanation: Linear parts never create new frequencies, so in steady state each quantity is a sine at the drive frequency: one complex phasor captures it.

question: In the DC MNA of Phase 05, what does a resistor R add to the matrix?
options: R on the diagonal
+1/R on the two diagonal entries of its nodes and -1/R on the two off-diagonal entries
A new row and column
Nothing, resistors only appear on the right-hand side
explanation: The conductance stamp: +G at (a,a) and (b,b), -G at (a,b) and (b,a). AC analysis uses the same stamp with a complex admittance.

question: What is the admittance of a 1 uF capacitor at omega = 1000 rad/s?
options: 1e-6 S
explanation: Y_C = j omega C = j x 1000 x 1e-6 = 0.001j S.

question: Why does our simple AC solver fail at exactly 0 Hz when the circuit contains an inductor?
options: Because resistors have no admittance at DC
Because numpy cannot solve complex systems
Because the source has no phase at DC
Because the inductor's admittance 1 / (j omega L) divides by zero
explanation: At omega = 0 an inductor is a perfect short with infinite admittance. Simulators avoid this by giving inductors their own current unknown.

question: Our solver and sim's AC analysis differ by about 1e-8 dB. What causes it?
options: A bug in one of them
sim adds a tiny gmin conductance from every node to ground
sim uses time steps
The capacitors have tolerance
explanation: gmin = 1e-12 S keeps the matrix solvable for floating nodes; at kilo-ohm impedance levels it changes results only in the eighth digit.

question: During AC analysis with V1 as the source, what happens to another independent DC voltage source in the circuit?
options: It is set to zero, so it behaves like a short circuit
It is removed, leaving an open circuit
It is added to V1
It doubles
explanation: By superposition, AC analysis drives one source at a time. Other voltage sources keep their branch but have zero value: a short.

question: An AC analysis says V(out) = 0.36 at +69 degrees at 1400 Hz. What does a transient simulation show after it settles?
options: A square wave
Nothing, transient and AC analyses are unrelated
A 1400 Hz sine of amplitude 0.36 leading the input by 69 degrees
A 2800 Hz sine
explanation: The phasor is a description of the steady-state sine: its size is the amplitude and its angle the phase relative to the input.
